Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ATHENS, Greece (CNN) -- Authorities vowed to re-impose order after demonstrators rose up across Greece Monday in a third day of rioting over Saturday's killing of a 15-year-old boy that has left dozens injured and scores of properties destroyed. An undated photo of Alexandros Grigoropoulos, whose death has sparked riots across Greece. "Under no circumstances will the government accept what is occurring," said Greek Interior Minister Prokopis Pavlopoulos. "We will do what is necessary." It was unclear what would be necessary to placate the demonstrators. "We've just lost count of how many demonstrations are taking place now," a police spokesman in Athens told CNN. Police said 34 civilians and 16 police officers were injured Monday in rioting that spread into new municipalities, including Trikala, Larissam and Veria. Riots broke out Saturday in Thessaloniki and Athens, where police killed the teen.  Watch the latest report on the rioting » . Demonstrators had torched three government buildings and three offices of the ruling conservative political party in downtown Athens, a National Fire Brigade spokesman told Greek state television. Watch as iReporter witnesses the clashes . Thirty-five cars and 160 trash containers also had been set ablaze, he said.  See images of anarchy on Greek streets » . Demonstrators Monday barricaded streets in Athens and Thessaloniki and hurled gasoline bombs as they battled with police. Clouds of tear gas hung over the capital city as riot police continued to battle the hundreds of young self-styled anarchists rioting over the boy's death. "Rage is what I feel for what has happened, rage, and that this cop who did it must see what it is to kill a kid and to destroy a life," a student in Athens told reporters Monday.  Watch protesters clash with police » . In a nationally televised address broadcast on state television, Greek Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis condemned the violence and promised to punish those responsible for Saturday's shooting. He also announced a decision to drop plans to reimburse business owners affected by the rioting. The police officer who fired the fatal shot has been charged with "manslaughter with intent" and suspended from duty, police said, adding that a second police officer was arrested Saturday on criminal accessory charges. Government officials have condemned the shooting. "An investigation is under way and those found responsible will be punished," said Pavlopoulos. "Measures will also be taken to avoid such incidents again in the future." iReport.com: Are you there? Share photos, video of rioting . On Monday, authorities conducted an autopsy on the teenage boy in an effort to answer questions about the circumstances of the shooting, but the boy's family has called in their own investigators to verify state findings, the Athens coroner told CNN. The U.S. and British embassies issued warnings to employees and tourists on Sunday, instructing them to avoid downtown Athens and other major cities until rioting subsides. Tourists in central Athens hotels were advised by hotel staff not to leave their rooms as police fanned out across the city. "There are lots of burning bins and debris in the street and a huge amount of tear gas in the air, which we got choked with on the way back to our hotel," according to Joel Brown, a CNN senior press officer visiting Athens on Sunday. A police statement about the teenage boy's death said the incident started when six young protesters pelted a police patrol car with stones. The teen was shot as he tried to throw a petrol bomb at the officers, police said. Other angry teens converged on the site almost immediately. Fighting between youths and police erupted elsewhere, including Thessaloniki, the country's second-largest city. Hundreds of young people took to the streets of the sprawling port city, finally barricading themselves behind the gates of a state university. Authorities have been barred from entering university grounds since tanks crushed a 1973 student uprising protesting the ruling military junta. It was not clear what authorities would do about the demonstrators still holed up at the university. No deaths have been reported since Saturday. Police said Monday that 20 protesters had been rounded up for questioning. Journalist Anthee Carassava in Athens contributed to this report.

**ATHENS, Greece (CNN) —** Authorities vowed to restore order after demonstrators rose up across Greece on Monday, marking a third day of rioting over Saturday’s killing of 15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos. The unrest has left dozens injured and scores of properties destroyed.

*An undated photograph of Alexandros Grigoropoulos, whose death sparked riots across Greece.*

“Under no circumstances will the government accept what is occurring,” Greek Interior Minister Prokopis Pavlopoulos said. “We will do what is necessary.”

It remained unclear what measures would be necessary to placate the demonstrators.

“We’ve just lost count of how many demonstrations are taking place now,” a police spokesman in Athens told CNN.

Police said 34 civilians and 16 officers were injured Monday as the rioting spread to additional municipalities, including Trikala, Larissa and Veria. The unrest began Saturday in Thessaloniki and Athens, where police killed the teenager.

*Watch the latest report on the rioting »*

Demonstrators torched three government buildings and three offices belonging to the ruling conservative political party in downtown Athens, a National Fire Brigade spokesman told Greek state television.

*Watch as an iReporter witnesses the clashes.*

Thirty-five cars and 160 trash containers were also set ablaze, the spokesman said.

*See images of anarchy on Greek streets »*

On Monday, demonstrators barricaded streets in Athens and Thessaloniki and hurled gasoline bombs as they battled police. Clouds of tear gas hung over the capital as riot police continued to confront hundreds of young, self-styled anarchists protesting the boy’s death.

“Rage is what I feel for what has happened—rage—and that this cop who did it must see what it is to kill a kid and to destroy a life,” a student in Athens told reporters Monday.

*Watch protesters clash with police »*

In a nationally televised address broadcast on state television, Greek Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis condemned the violence and promised to punish those responsible for Saturday’s shooting. He also announced a decision to abandon plans to reimburse business owners affected by the rioting.

The officer who fired the fatal shot has been charged with “manslaughter with intent” and suspended from duty, police said. A second officer was arrested Saturday on charges of being a criminal accessory.

Government officials condemned the shooting.

“An investigation is under way, and those found responsible will be punished,” Pavlopoulos said. “Measures will also be taken to avoid such incidents again in the future.”

*iReport.com: Are you there? Share photos and video of the rioting.*

Authorities conducted an autopsy on the teenager Monday in an effort to answer questions about the circumstances of the shooting. However, the boy’s family brought in its own investigators to verify the state’s findings, the Athens coroner told CNN.

The U.S. and British embassies issued warnings to employees and tourists Sunday, instructing them to avoid downtown Athens and other major cities until the unrest subsided. Hotel staff advised tourists staying in central Athens not to leave their rooms as police spread across the city.

“There are lots of burning bins and debris in the street and a huge amount of tear gas in the air, which we got choked with on the way back to our hotel,” said Joel Brown, a CNN senior press officer who was visiting Athens on Sunday.

A police statement concerning the teenager’s death said the incident began when six young protesters pelted a police patrol car with stones. Police said the teenager was shot while attempting to throw a petrol bomb at the officers.

Other angry teenagers converged on the scene almost immediately, and clashes between youths and police erupted elsewhere, including in Thessaloniki, the country’s second-largest city.

Hundreds of young people took to the streets of the sprawling port city before barricading themselves behind the gates of a state university. Authorities have been barred from entering university grounds since tanks crushed a 1973 student uprising against the ruling military junta.

It remained unclear what action authorities would take regarding the demonstrators still barricaded inside the university.

No deaths have been reported since Saturday. Police said Monday that 20 protesters had been detained for questioning.

Journalist Anthee Carassava in Athens contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
ATHENS, Greece (CNN) — Greek officials pledged to restore public order Monday as unrest spread nationwide for a third consecutive day following the fatal police shooting of 15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos on Saturday. The violence has injured dozens of people and damaged or destroyed numerous properties. An undated photograph showed Grigoropoulos, whose death triggered the disturbances.

Greek Interior Minister Prokopis Pavlopoulos said the government would not tolerate the situation under any circumstances and would take whatever action was required. However, it remained uncertain what steps might calm the protesters.

An Athens police spokesman told CNN that authorities could no longer keep track of the number of demonstrations under way. Police reported that Monday’s violence had expanded to additional municipalities, including Trikala, Larissam and Veria, leaving 34 civilians and 16 officers injured.

The rioting began Saturday in Athens, where the teenager was killed by police, and in Thessaloniki. CNN provided video coverage of the latest unrest.

According to a National Fire Brigade spokesman speaking to Greek state television, protesters set fire to three government buildings and three offices belonging to the governing conservative party in central Athens. CNN also featured eyewitness footage submitted by an iReporter. The spokesman added that 35 vehicles and 160 garbage containers had been burned. Images of the turmoil in Greek streets were also made available.

On Monday, protesters blocked roads in Athens and Thessaloniki, threw gasoline bombs and fought with police. Tear gas filled the air over the capital as riot officers confronted hundreds of young demonstrators who described themselves as anarchists and were protesting the teenager’s death.

One Athens student told journalists that the shooting had left them feeling intense anger and that the officer responsible should understand what it meant to kill a child and end a life. Video showed protesters clashing with police.

In a speech carried nationwide on state television, Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis denounced the violence and promised that those responsible for Saturday’s shooting would be punished. He also said plans to compensate business owners whose properties had been affected by the riots would be abandoned.

Police said the officer who fired the fatal bullet had been suspended and charged with “manslaughter with intent.” A second officer was arrested Saturday and accused of being a criminal accessory.

Government representatives criticized the shooting. Pavlopoulos said an inquiry was in progress, anyone found accountable would face punishment, and measures would be introduced to prevent similar incidents in the future. CNN’s iReport invited people at the scene to submit photographs and video of the unrest.

Authorities performed an autopsy on Grigoropoulos on Monday to clarify the circumstances surrounding his death. The Athens coroner told CNN that the boy’s family had hired independent investigators to check the official findings.

On Sunday, the American and British embassies warned staff members and visitors to stay away from central Athens and other large Greek cities until the disorder ended. Hotel employees advised tourists staying in downtown Athens not to leave their rooms while police deployed throughout the city.

Joel Brown, a CNN senior press officer visiting Athens on Sunday, described streets filled with burning garbage bins and debris. He said the air contained so much tear gas that he and others were choking as they returned to their hotel.

In an official account of the teenager’s death, police said the confrontation began when six young protesters threw stones at a patrol car. According to police, Grigoropoulos was shot while attempting to hurl a petrol bomb at the officers.

Other enraged teenagers arrived at the location almost at once. Confrontations between young people and police then broke out in other places, including Thessaloniki, Greece’s second-largest city.

Hundreds of youths entered the streets of the large port city before eventually taking refuge behind the gates of a state university. Police and other authorities have been prohibited from entering university campuses since military tanks crushed a student revolt against Greece’s ruling junta in 1973.

Officials had not indicated how they intended to deal with the protesters who remained inside the university. No additional fatalities had been reported since Saturday. Police said Monday that 20 demonstrators had been detained for questioning.

CNN journalist Anthee Carassava contributed reporting from Athens.

Riots spread across Greece for a third consecutive day after the fatal police shooting of 15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos in Athens. The teenager was killed in the Exarchia district, an area long associated with student activism and clashes between anarchist groups and police. His death triggered an immediate wave of anger, with demonstrations quickly escalating into some of the country’s most serious civil unrest in years.

Protesters erected barricades, set fire to cars and buildings, smashed shop windows, and threw stones and gasoline bombs at police. Officers responded with tear gas and deployed riot units in an effort to regain control. Although the most intense confrontations took place in Athens, disturbances and solidarity demonstrations were also reported in other Greek cities.

At least 50 people were injured during the unrest. Government buildings, political party offices, businesses, vehicles, and other property were damaged or destroyed, leaving streets littered with broken glass and burned debris. The scale of the destruction placed growing pressure on the government to contain the violence while addressing public outrage over the shooting.

Greek authorities vowed to restore order and hold those responsible for the teenager’s death accountable. The officers involved were detained, and officials promised a full investigation. Protesters, students, and opposition groups nevertheless demanded swift punishment, arguing that the shooting reflected broader problems of police conduct and government accountability.

The continuing unrest highlighted deep frustration among many young Greeks and intensified criticism of the government. What began as anger over a single fatal encounter rapidly developed into a wider expression of public rage, leaving the authorities facing both a security crisis and mounting demands for justice.

**Athens, Greece: Where Ancient History Meets Modern Life**

ATHENS, Greece (CNN) — Few cities blend the ancient and the modern as vividly as Athens. Dominated by the Acropolis and the iconic Parthenon, the Greek capital offers visitors a direct connection to more than 2,500 years of history.

Beyond its archaeological landmarks, Athens is a lively Mediterranean metropolis. Neighborhoods such as Plaka and Monastiraki are filled with cafés, restaurants and small shops, while areas like Psyrri showcase the city’s street art and nightlife. Traditional tavernas serve Greek favorites including souvlaki, moussaka and fresh seafood.

Athens also serves as a gateway to Greece’s islands and coastal destinations. From the nearby port of Piraeus, ferries carry travelers to Santorini, Mykonos, Crete and many other islands.

With its historic monuments, energetic cultural scene and warm climate, Athens remains one of Europe’s most distinctive capitals—a city where the legacy of the ancient world continues to shape everyday life.

- **Property damage:** Protesters threw rocks and Molotov cocktails, set fire to **cars, banks, shops and public buildings**, smashed storefronts and looted businesses. Damage was reported in Athens and other Greek cities.
- **Government response:** Prime Minister **Costas Karamanlis** condemned the rioting, promised that those responsible for the teenager’s death would be punished, and said the government would protect citizens and property. Interior Minister **Prokopis Pavlopoulos** offered to resign, but Karamanlis refused to accept the resignation. The government also rejected suggestions that it had lost control or would declare a state of emergency.
- **Police actions:** Riot police used **tear gas** against stone- and firebomb-throwing demonstrators, made arrests and placed officers around government buildings and central Athens. The officer accused of firing the fatal shot was charged with **intentional homicide**, while a second officer was charged as an accomplice. Police said warning shots had been fired and that the bullet may have ricocheted, a version disputed by witnesses.

counterfactuals.output:
## BREAKING NEWS: Greece Erupts After Police Shooting of 15-Year-Old Boy

**ATHENS, Greece —** Violent protests have spread across Greece after a police officer fatally shot a 15-year-old boy in central Athens, triggering some of the country’s most intense civil unrest in years.

The teenager, identified as **Alexandros “Alexis” Grigoropoulos**, was killed Saturday night in **Exarchia**, an Athens neighborhood known for its student population and history of clashes between anarchist groups and police.

Within hours, demonstrators took to the streets of Athens, smashing storefronts, setting vehicles and banks on fire and confronting riot police. The unrest quickly spread to **Thessaloniki**, Greece’s second-largest city, and to Patras, Ioannina, Larissa, Volos, Heraklion and other urban centers.

### Conflicting accounts of the shooting

Greek authorities say two police special guards encountered a group of youths in Exarchia after an apparent verbal confrontation. One officer fired his weapon, striking Grigoropoulos.

The officer reportedly claimed he fired warning shots and that a bullet ricocheted. Witnesses and protesters have challenged that account, alleging the teenager was deliberately shot during the confrontation.

Both officers have been detained. The officer who fired the fatal shot faces a homicide accusation, while his partner is being investigated in connection with the killing. Authorities have ordered a forensic examination and ballistic tests to establish the bullet’s trajectory.

The precise circumstances remain under investigation.

### Athens engulfed in violence

In the capital, thick smoke has risen over major commercial districts as groups of masked youths have hurled rocks and firebombs at police. Riot officers have responded with repeated volleys of tear gas.

Cars, garbage containers and barricades have been set ablaze. Banks, government buildings and shops have been attacked, with extensive damage reported near Exarchia, Syntagma Square and central shopping streets.

Firefighters have struggled to reach some burning buildings because of continuing confrontations. Residents and tourists have been urged to avoid the city center, while public transportation has faced delays and disruptions.

Students have occupied or gathered at schools and universities, turning several campuses into organizing centers for demonstrations. Greek universities traditionally have strong restrictions on police entry, making them frequent rallying points during periods of unrest.

### Clashes spread to Thessaloniki and beyond

In **Thessaloniki**, demonstrators have attacked shops and banks and clashed with police near the city center and university district. Fires have been reported as riot police attempt to disperse crowds with tear gas.

Protests have also broken out in several smaller cities. Police stations and government offices have been targeted in some locations, while solidarity demonstrations have been reported on Greek islands and in communities far from Athens.

The unrest is no longer confined to anarchist groups. Students, labor organizations and ordinary residents have joined marches condemning police violence and demanding accountability for the teenager’s death.

### Government appeals for calm

Prime Minister **Kostas Karamanlis** has expressed condolences to the boy’s family and promised a full investigation. His government has appealed for calm while condemning the destruction of public and private property.

The interior minister and senior police officials have come under growing pressure over the shooting and the authorities’ response. Opposition parties are accusing the government of failing to control the police and of allowing public anger—already fueled by economic hardship, unemployment and political scandals—to reach a breaking point.

The government faces a difficult balance: restoring order without intensifying outrage over the teenager’s death.

### A nation in shock

The killing has become a rallying point for young Greeks frustrated by unemployment, limited economic opportunities and distrust of state institutions. For many protesters, Grigoropoulos’ death represents more than an isolated police shooting; it has become a symbol of deeper anger toward the government and law enforcement.

Schools and universities are expected to remain central to the demonstrations, and unions and opposition groups are calling for further marches. Authorities are deploying additional riot police as Greece prepares for the possibility of more violence.

The investigation into the shooting continues, but the teenager’s death has already ignited a nationwide crisis—one unfolding in burning streets from Athens to Thessaloniki and across the country.
